issues.legal_issue: A post-notification delay in issuing an acquisition declaration does not, by itself, invalidate the decision to dispense with an objection inquiry when the acquisition addresses an established urgent housing need and there is no other material undermining that decision.
material_facts: The acquisition was for a planned residential development intended to address an acute shortage of housing.
Before the notification, officials had submitted reports and certificates identifying the need and urgency of the housing scheme.
The declaration followed the notification by nearly a year because officials processing the case had made errors that required correction.
There was no allegation of bad faith, and the landowners did not dispute the urgent need for housing.
issues.conclusion: The post-notification delay alone did not make the decision to dispense with the inquiry improper or illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5-A and 17(1) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the State may dispense with the inquiry in an urgent acquisition. Applying Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor of Delhi and the housing-urgency reasoning quoted from Kasireddy Papaiah, the Court held that bureaucratic delay alone does not undo an otherwise justified urgency decision absent bad faith or other material undermining it. Narayan Govind Gavate v. State of Maharashtra was distinguished in light of the changed urgency of providing housing amid population growth.

predicates.appeal_against_quashing_of_land_acquisit: The matter is an appeal challenging a decision that quashed a land acquisition.
predicates.urgent_housing_need_supported_by_materia: Officials provided material showing an urgent need for housing accommodation.
predicates.post_notification_delay_due_to_official_: Officials' errors in processing the matter caused a delay after the acquisition notification.
predicates.no_bad_faith_or_other_material_undermini: No bad faith or other material was shown that undermined the stated urgency.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges the quashing of an acquisition, supported urgent housing need and an official-error delay, without bad faith or other contrary material, lead to the urgency dispensation remaining valid.

issues.legal_issue: A few structures within a large tract acquired for urgent planned urban development do not require the structured portions to be excluded from the development scheme, and the land's general nature and condition determine whether it is waste or arable.
material_facts: The acquisition covered a large tract for planned urban development.
The tract was generally described as arable, although a few structures stood on small portions of it.
Separating the small built-up portions from the rest would impede applying the urgent acquisition process consistently across the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The presence of a few structures did not justify excluding those small portions from the acquisition; the general nature and condition of the land govern its characterization as waste or arable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 17(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and held that, for a large urgent planned-development scheme, it would not be proper to leave small portions containing superstructures outside the scheme. Whether land is waste or arable is assessed by its general nature and condition.

predicates.urgent_planned_urban_development: The land is being acquired for an urgent planned urban-development scheme.
predicates.large_tract_acquired: The acquisition covers a large tract of land.
predicates.only_small_portions_have_structures: Structures stand on only small portions of the larger tract.

issues.definition: In an urgent planned urban-development acquisition of a large tract, structures confined to small portions do not require those portions to be excluded.

issues.legal_issue: When land is acquired for planned development and the urgency power is invoked, possession may be taken of land that is neither waste nor arable, and failure to expressly cite the applicable possession power in the notification is not fatal.
material_facts: The acquisition was for planned development.
The notification invoked the urgency power but did not expressly refer to the provision authorizing possession of land other than waste or arable land.
The land included some portions with structures.
issues.conclusion: The omission to refer expressly to the additional possession power did not invalidate the acquisition; the Government could take possession of non-waste and non-arable land for planned development when the urgency power was invoked.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1-A), as inserted by the Land Acquisition (U.P. Amendment) Act, 1954, permits possession of land other than waste or arable land when it is acquired for sanitary improvements or planned development. The Court held that invoking section 17(1) in a planned-development acquisition attracts that power without a further declaration, and that omission to cite section 17(1-A) expressly in the notification is not fatal.

predicates.planned_development_acquisition: The land is acquired for planned development.
predicates.urgency_power_invoked: The Government invokes the urgency power in the acquisition.
predicates.notification_omits_express_reference_to_: The notification does not expressly refer to the power permitting possession of land that is neither waste nor arable.

issues.definition: For a planned-development acquisition in which the urgency power is invoked, omitting an express reference to the non-arable-land possession power does not prevent possession of that land.

issues.legal_issue: A development authority acquiring a large tract for urban development should, so far as practicable, provide suitable accommodation on reasonable terms to displaced owners who lack homes or shop buildings.
material_facts: A development authority acquired a large tract to provide residential accommodation through urban development.
Some people whose land was acquired might have no houses or shop buildings in the urban area and could face serious prejudice.

A provision in another development statute afforded an opportunity for suitable accommodation to people living or carrying on activities on acquired land, although that provision did not apply directly to this acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The Court stated that the principle in the other development statute should guide development authorities and expressed the hope that the acquiring authority would, as far as practicable, offer a reasonable house site or shop site on reasonable terms to affected people lacking houses or shop buildings.
issues.legal_principle: Although section 21(2) of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 did not apply to the acquisition, the Court treated its accommodation principle as a wholesome one that development authorities throughout the country should follow when acquiring large tracts for urban development.

predicates.urban_land_acquisition_by_development_au: A development authority acquires land for urban development.
predicates.large_tract_acquired: The acquisition covers a large tract of land.
predicates.displaced_people_lack_homes_or_shop_buil: Some people whose land is acquired lack homes or shop buildings in the urban area.

issues.definition: When a development authority acquires a large urban tract and displaces people who lack homes or shop buildings, it should practicably offer them a suitable site on reasonable terms.
